text: Chapter 1 was honest that CMDB data quality is genuinely hard, and that nothing about Discovery or the rules covered in the last two lessons makes it automatically stay good forever. This lesson follows through on that framing with the real, well-documented reason most CMDB implementations actually fail in practice -- and it's almost never a technical platform limitation.

Discovery gets configured, Identification and Reconciliation rules get tuned carefully, an initial cleanup runs, and the Health Dashboard shows a great score on launch day. Then, six to twelve months later, nobody is specifically accountable for keeping it that way, and the score quietly slides back down. The platform didn't fail -- the governance around it was simply never built. The real fix is unglamorous and specific: a named individual Business or Technical Service Owner for each service, and a named CI-class data owner accountable for that class's accuracy across the entire CMDB -- not a team, not 'IT' in the abstract, one specific person.

A Business or Technical Service Owner is accountable for whether that service's representation in the CMDB -- its CIs, its dependency mapping, its relationships to the business capabilities it supports -- stays accurate as the service itself changes over time. A CI-class data owner is accountable for a specific class's data quality everywhere in the CMDB, regardless of which business service any individual CI happens to support -- the person who owns server CI quality cares about every server, not just the ones tied to one application.

Ownership without a schedule tends to collapse into 'I'll get to it eventually.' A real governance model defines a recurring review cadence, commonly quarterly, where each owner reviews their current Health Dashboard scores, confirms whether flagged duplicate pairs actually got merged, and signs off that their data is still accurate -- or opens a remediation item if it isn't. This is the mechanism that closes the loop from the dashboard two lessons back: a score alone doesn't fix anything, but a score plus a named owner plus a scheduled review genuinely does.

None of this replaces Discovery or the Identification and Reconciliation rules -- those remain the actual technical mechanisms producing accurate data in the first place. But technical configuration alone has no memory and no accountability; left alone, it will happily let a correct CMDB decay the moment nobody is watching the dashboard. Governance is what gives that configuration a reason to stay correct long after the initial build. Next up: a worked lab pulling identification, cleanup, and ownership together into one real scenario.
